claims.statement: The application selects one of four run modes from process.argv at module load: the default entry is the windowless outer guard, `--panel` is the panel main process, `--accept` is the acceptance battery controller, and `--icon-restore` is a one-shot icon-restore entry whose branch runs before any single-instance logic.

Two dispatch steps are hard pre-`app.whenReady()` constraints: `registerPluginScheme()` must run before ready because Electron requires privileged scheme registration at that point, and the guard's `app.disableHardwareAcceleration()` is pre-ready-only because the guard opens no window and must not carry a GPU process.

In `--accept` mode the process takes no single-instance lock, replaces the default window-all-closed quit with an empty handler so the controller outlives its own windows, and runs `accept/battery.js` inside the same Electron app context so the battery can spawn real guard/panel processes while remaining a controller.

Single-instance admission is a two-lock handoff: the guard requests the lock first and logs `single-instance-refused` then quits when refused, but it releases the lock before spawning so a still-shutting-down previous instance cannot be mistaken for a second launch; the panel child re-acquires the lock and holds it until exit, so at most one panel is on screen even during the release window.

The guard is deliberately the parent of the panel process: `taskkill /T` clears only the downward subtree, so killing or crashing the panel cannot reach the guard and the process that hid the desktop icons survives to restore them; because the restore duty lives in the guard rather than the panel, `npm run dev:panel` can run `electron . --panel` directly with no icon hiding and no restore.

The guard spawns its child as `spawn(process.execPath, [app.getAppPath(), '--panel'], { cwd: app.getAppPath(), env: process.env, stdio: 'inherit' })`, so the panel inherits the guard's environment (including `DECK_EVENT_LOG`) and its console, and is launched by the same Electron binary that booted the guard.

Both guard terminal paths restore the native icons before ending the guard: a spawn error restores with reason `panel-spawn-failed` and exits 1, while child exit restores with reason `panel-exit` and then calls `app.exit(code)` with the child's exit code — the explicit restore being necessary because `app.exit` skips the normal quit sequence.

The detached restore watcher is spawned by the guard only when the guard actually hid the icons (`carry.didHide()`), with `detached: true`, `stdio: 'ignore'` and `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1`, and is `unref()`ed so it neither holds the guard open nor can be reached by the console signal that kills guard and panel together.

`bootPanel()` boots in a fixed order — evidence log, config load, autostart, legacy usage-log migration, kernel start, then window — and the window is only created after `await kernel.panelData.whenReady`, i.e. after the data plane's first snapshot, with a 15 s timeout that lets the panel start with an empty data plane rather than not at all.

The panel window is created with `show: false`, `frame: false`, `transparent: true`, `backgroundColor: '#00000000'`, `hasShadow: false`, `resizable: false` and `movable: false`, plus a sandboxed preload-only renderer (`contextIsolation: true`, `sandbox: true`, `nodeIntegration: false`), and geometry taken from `config.panel`, which defaults to the primary display's bounds.

`focusable: false` (Windows `WS_EX_NOACTIVATE`) means the panel can never activate — a click neither raises it nor steals the keyboard from the user's working window — and `skipTaskbar: true` removes the taskbar button and makes Win11's ToggleDesktop exempt the panel from Win+D, so the debounce restorer is a safety net rather than the primary defense.

The panel becomes visible exclusively through `win.showInactive()`: once at startup from the `ready-to-show` handler (registered before `win.loadURL(panelUrl())`) and thereafter on every recall, so showing the panel never takes focus.

ADR-0005's red line is that the window-host thread holds no system-level input hook: `setIgnoreMouseEvents(true)` is called without `forward`, because forwarding makes Electron install a global `WH_MOUSE_LL` low-level mouse hook on the main thread that every system mouse event must wait on, and hover highlight is driven by real events only after pass-through has been lifted.

Interactivity is declared by the renderer and enforced by the main process: `window.deck.host.setHotZones(rects)` sends `{ id, x, y, w, h }` rectangles relative to the client area's top-left in CSS px (= DIP) over the fire-and-forget `deck:host-set-hotzones` channel to `HotzoneTracker.setRects()`.

`HotzoneTracker` polls every 25 ms: it converts `screen.getCursorScreenPoint()` into window-relative coordinates by subtracting `win.getBounds()`, calls `setIgnoreMouseEvents(false)` on the entering edge when any declared rectangle contains the point, and restores pass-through only after two consecutive misses (`LEAVE_CONFIRM_POLLS = 2`), disposing itself when the window is destroyed.

The hotzone leave hook re-pins the window to the bottom but is throttled to at most one call per 500 ms, because each `SetWindowPos(..., HWND_BOTTOM, ...)` makes Windows re-evaluate the whole z-order and boundary jitter must not become a z-order storm.

The renderer declares one hotzone per `.card`, one per desktop zone, and one each for the settings button and the overlay's reset button, filters out zero-area rectangles, and derives a zone rectangle from the union of its item boxes plus a 10 px margin intersected with the visible container — so an empty zone produces no rectangle and therefore no click dead zone.

Hotzones are re-declared whenever the layout can have moved: after every snapshot render, on `plugins/changed`, on settings open/close, on search activate/deactivate, and once `document.fonts.ready` resolves, which is why a plugin card becomes clickable by carrying the shared `card` class and an id on its own element.

Bottom pinning is a koffi FFI call into `user32.dll`: `SetWindowPos(hwndOf(win), HWND_BOTTOM, 0, 0, 0, 0, SWP_NOMOVE | SWP_NOSIZE | SWP_NOACTIVATE | SWP_NOOWNERZORDER)`, with the HWND obtained by decoding `win.getNativeWindowHandle()` as `uintptr_t`, because Electron has no native always-at-the-bottom level.

The bottom is re-asserted at window start (`ready-to-show`, reason `startup`), on every recall (reason `show-<recall reason>`), on hotzone leave (reason `hotzone-leave`), on stray `focus` events (reason `focus-fallback`), and on both keyboard-mode switches; only a successful pin is written to the evidence log because the log append sits inside `if (pinToBottom(win))`.

ADR-0004 fixes the stacking order as background layer < panel < ordinary windows, so the panel sits above the user's wallpaper and below every ordinary window — including while keyboard mode has made it the foreground window.

Keyboard mode is one host-channel switch: on performs `win.setFocusable(true)` then `win.focus()` then `pinToBottom(win)`, off performs `win.setFocusable(false)` then `pinToBottom(win)`, each writing a `keyboard-mode-on` / `keyboard-mode-off` evidence event, and a destroyed window is ignored.

Turning keyboard mode off deliberately does not restore focus to the previously focused window (the same semantics as clicking the real desktop), and both the search overlay and the settings overlay drive the switch as on/off pairs from the renderer, with the off call guarded by the overlay's own open flag.

All recall paths converge on one implementation, `showPanel(reason)` = restore if minimized or hidden via `showInactive()` → re-pin → log `panel-shown` with the reason; the three callers are tray click (`tray-click`), `app.on('second-instance')` registered in the lock-holding panel process (`second-instance`), and the Win+D restorer's expiry (`wind-restore`).

The tray icon is drawn programmatically as a 32 px BGRA bitmap (dark background plus four amber `#f5a623` squares) so no binary asset ships, its left click recalls the panel, its context menu's `退出面板` item quits, and it is destroyed in `before-quit` so the icon cannot outlive the process.

`WinDRestorer` polls its injected down-predicate every 250 ms and starts a 1500 ms debounce timer on the first hit of an episode; repeated hits during one episode do not restart the timer, leaving the down state cancels the episode, restore fires only if the predicate still reports down at expiry (passing the measured `afterMs`), and `dispose()` clears both the interval and the pending timer.

The production Win+D predicate watches `win.isMinimized()` only and never returns `'hidden'`; `!isVisible` is deliberately not watched because hidden is the legitimate pre-show state and any future hide-the-panel feature must not be overridden by the restorer.

Quit teardown is explicit: `win.on('closed')` disposes the hotzone tracker and the Win+D restorer, `window-all-closed` calls `app.quit()`, `before-quit` logs `quit` and destroys the tray, and the panel's exit code then reaches the guard, which restores the native icons and exits with that same code — the panel never restores icons itself.

`config.panel` is read once per boot and applied to the window, and because the window is neither movable nor resizable a geometry change requires a panel restart; illegal field values fall back to the default per field with a warning rather than silently.

The window host's behaviour is observable only when `DECK_EVENT_LOG` is set, because `fileEventLog` returns null otherwise; the events it records for this area are `boot`, `pin` (with reason `startup`, `show-*`, `hotzone-leave` or `focus-fallback`), `panel-shown`, `hotzones`, `hotzone-enter`/`hotzone-leave`, `keyboard-mode-on`/`keyboard-mode-off`, `wind-minimized`/`wind-restored`, `single-instance-refused` and `quit`.

`app/tests/wind-restore.spec.ts` is the only offline unit test in this area, driving `WinDRestorer` with injected predicate/hooks and fake timers (including `Date`, because the episode start is wall-clock) to pin single-`onMinimized`-per-episode, no-early-restore, restore-at-expiry with `afterMs`, cancellation on state clear, no timer reset on repeated hits, and silence after `dispose()`.

Window behaviour has no offline test by design and is verified by the real-machine acceptance battery, which asserts window state rather than module behaviour: `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT | WS_EX_LAYERED` plus clicks reaching the desktop, a hotzone style flip in both directions, a click that neither raises nor activates the panel, panel index below the notepad, second-launch refusal, tray registration and amber-pixel visibility, Win+D immunity plus `SW_MINIMIZE` debounce restore, and keyboard-mode on/off for both overlays.

The battery drives the production entry chain rather than production modules: it spawns `electron .` (the guard, so the whole spawn chain including icon carry is under test) with `DECK_EVENT_LOG` pointed at `accept/evidence/03-runtime-events.jsonl`, and uses its own `accept/lib/win32.js` helpers for window probing and for the `WM_CLOSE` exit-pipeline check.
